## Primary resistance to single and multiple drugs in leprosy: a mouse footpad study

Skin biopsy homogenates obtained from three cases of lepromatous leprosy with no prior history of antileprosy treatment were tested in the mouse footpad for the sensitivity of _Mycobacterium leprae_ to multiple drugs. Footpads were inoculated with the homogenates and subsequently treated with a range of drug concentrations, individually and in combination, mimicking common leprosy treatment regimens.  Growth inhibition was assessed by measuring footpad swelling at various time points. The results demonstrated that _M. leprae_ isolates from all three patients exhibited varying degrees of primary resistance to multiple drugs, including rifampicin, dapsone, clofazimine, and ofloxacin. Notably, isolates from two patients showed high-level resistance to two or more drugs, highlighting the potential for inherent drug resistance in untreated leprosy patients. This murine footpad model provides a valuable tool for investigating the mechanisms underlying primary drug resistance in leprosy and for developing strategies to address this growing public health concern.

The lack of effect of melatonin suggests distinct mechanisms of action for these two indoleamines in regulating the ovulatory process. ## A Reinvestigation of Two Critical Points in the Energetics of Muscular Contraction

Two critical points in the energetics of muscular contraction have been re-examined: (1) the absence of heat production after the active state has ended (i.e. in 'relaxation') and (2) the mobilization of stored energy during isometric contractions. 

While previously considered straightforward, recent advances in calorimetric and biomechanical techniques allow for a deeper understanding of these processes.  This study utilizes a novel in vitro model combined with precise calorimetric measurements and force transduction to investigate the subtle energy fluxes during both contraction and relaxation phases. We demonstrate that the absence of heat production during relaxation is not absolute, revealing a low-level metabolic cost associated with maintaining muscle readiness for reactivation. Furthermore, we challenge the prevailing notion of solely ATP-driven energy utilization during isometric contractions, providing evidence for a significant contribution from stored elastic energy. These findings offer a refined understanding of the complex interplay between mechanical work, chemical energy utilization, and elastic storage within the muscle tissue.  Implications for understanding energy efficiency and potential therapeutic targets for muscle-related disorders are discussed.
